title: Evaluation: golden sets, offline scoring, human review, regression gates
story:
Without a set of cases, every change to one of these systems is an opinion, and opinions are settled by whoever speaks last. That is the entire reason evaluation exists here, and it is worth stating before any technique, because most teams do not lack a technique — they lack twenty examples with expected answers.

So start there and start small. Twenty real inputs, with what a good response would contain written next to each, is enough to catch the majority of regressions people actually ship. It does not need to be representative, comprehensive, or statistically defensible to be useful; it needs to exist and be re-run. Teams spend months designing the evaluation they will build later, while shipping unmeasured changes in the meantime, and the small ugly set that runs today beats the excellent one that does not exist yet.

Choose the cases by where the system has actually failed, not by what is typical. A set built from typical inputs measures the thing you are least worried about. A set built from real failures — the question that was answered from the wrong document, the one that returned nothing, the one where the answer was confident and wrong, the one that refused for no reason — measures your actual risk, and grows naturally because every incident contributes a case.

Then the question of scoring, which is where this gets hard. Some things are checkable: the answer contains the right identifier, the citation verifies, the output parses, the refusal happened when it should. Automate those, and be pleased at how many of your real failures they catch. What is left is judgement, and judgement has to be made repeatable: write down what a good answer must contain rather than what it should feel like, so two people scoring the same output agree. If you cannot write that down, you do not yet know what you want, and that is the thing to fix first.

A model can do some of the scoring, and the caution is specific rather than general. A model judging output is a model with all the same weaknesses as the one being judged — it prefers fluency, it prefers confidence, it prefers longer, and it will not notice a claim that is plausible and false any more reliably than a person skimming. It is reasonable for coarse checks over volume, and it is not reasonable as the only thing standing between a regression and your users. Calibrate it once against human scores on a sample, and re-check that agreement occasionally, or you are trusting a measurement you never validated.

Offline scoring and human review answer different questions and neither replaces the other. Offline scoring tells you whether a change broke something you already knew to care about, in minutes, on demand. Human review tells you what you did not know to care about, slowly, in small quantities. Keep both — a weekly read of sampled real traffic is what feeds new cases into the offline set, which is how the set stays relevant instead of ossifying around last year's problems.

And once the set exists, make it a gate rather than a report. A number produced in an afternoon and discussed in a meeting changes nothing. The same number, blocking a deploy when it drops, changes everything about how carefully people make changes. That transition — from measurement to gate — is the difference between a team that has evaluation and a team that does evaluation, and it costs nothing but the decision to enforce it.

problem.name: Measuring a change to a non-deterministic system
problem.shape: Changes have to be compared, and the output is different every time and judged rather than checked.
tell: changes are defended with a single impressive example
the evaluation everyone agrees is needed is still being designed
the cases were chosen because they are typical rather than because they failed
a score is produced and discussed but nothing is blocked by it
a model grades the output and nobody checked whether it agrees with a person
problem.move: Build twenty real cases with expected content, drawn from actual failures, automate whatever is checkable, write down what a good answer must contain for the rest, and make the set a gate that blocks a deploy rather than a report that gets discussed.
problem.invariant: A change is only an improvement relative to a fixed set of cases run before and after, because a single example cannot separate improvement from variation.
problem.breaks: A model used as a judge shares the weaknesses of the model being judged — preferring fluency, confidence and length — so it needs calibration against human scores before it is trusted alone.

cost.time: cases have to be written and maintained, and human review is slow and cannot be scaled
cost.space: the set is a small corpus with expected answers that needs to stay current as the product changes
cost.beats: trying it and seeing, which measures nothing, and a large formal benchmark, which arrives too late and measures somebody else's task

problem.practice: Open your incident notes or your support messages and pull out the last ten complaints about a wrong answer. Write each as an input with what the answer should have contained. That is your evaluation set, it took an hour, and it is aimed precisely at the failures you have already proven you can produce.

beats.broke: With no fixed set of cases, every change is judged on an example or two, so improvement and variation are indistinguishable and the loudest opinion wins.
beats.fix: Twenty real cases drawn from actual failures, with expected content, automated where checkable and written down where not, re-run on every change.
beats.cost: Cases need writing and maintaining, judgement has to be made repeatable, and a model used as judge must be calibrated against people before it is trusted.
